sections.b: Jubilees opens with two sets of tablets. Moses goes up Sinai for the stone tablets of the law (1:1), but the angel of the presence takes other tablets, "the tablets of the division of the years" (1:29), and dictates the book's dates from them. From 3:10 on the book speaks of "the heavenly tablets" where laws are written before they are given: the days of purity after childbirth (3:10) and the rule of punishment in kind (4:32). The same tablets are meant where the Ge'ez says only "the tablets," at the covering of nakedness (3:31), and at the curse on secret murder (4:5), where the transcribed Ge'ez has a slip and Dillmann's edition reads "the tablets of heaven." Each law is tied to a story in Genesis. Charles (1902) describes the tablets in Jubilees as the heavenly law book of which the law of Moses is the copy on earth, and also as a record of events and of what is to come.

sections.h: Jubilees 1-4: the calendar built into creation
sections.b: Jubilees counts history in weeks of seven years and jubilees of 49. Its opening prophecy lists Israel's coming sin as going wrong about "the start of the month and about Sabbaths, feasts, jubilees and ordinances" (1:14). In the creation story only the sun is the sign for days, months, feasts and years (2:9), where Genesis 1:14 gives the task to both lights. Enoch is the first to write down the signs of the sky by their months (4:17-18), and the angels say they taught him. The full defense of the 364-day year comes in Jubilees 6:23-38.

The book of Jubilees takes its name from its dating system. Its jubilee is seven weeks of years, 49 years, not the fiftieth year of Leviticus 25:8-11. Its arithmetic shows it: Adam dies at the end of the nineteenth jubilee, in the seventh week, in its sixth year (Jubilees 4:29), which is year 930, the 930 years of Genesis 5:5.

sections.h: Jubilees 2: the Sabbath kept in heaven
sections.b: In Jubilees the Sabbath is first a sign given to the two highest ranks of angels, who keep it with God in heaven (2:17-18, 30). God promises to set apart one people from the nations, Jacob's descendants, to keep it with them on earth (2:19-21, 31). Jacob is the twenty-second head of humankind as there were twenty-two works of creation (2:23). The chapter ends with a strict law: death for work, no cooking or drawing water, no carrying loads through the gates or from house to house, and a day of eating, drinking and blessing God (2:25-33).

common: Jubilees teaches that the Sabbath was kept by the angels before it was given to Israel.

sections.h: Jubilees 1-4: the angels of the presence
sections.b: Jubilees is told by "the angel of the presence," who went before Israel's camp (1:27-29; Exodus 14:19). The angels are made on the first day of creation (2:2): the angels of the presence and of holiness, who keep the Sabbath with God (2:18), and lower angels over fire, wind, cloud and season. The angels bring the animals to Adam (3:1), teach him to farm (3:15), report every sin to God (4:6), and, as the Watchers, are sent to teach justice on earth (4:15). The angel who writes for Moses is the earliest clear form of the belief that the law came through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2).

sections.b: In Jubilees the Watchers come down in Jared's days, as in 1 Enoch 6:6, but they are sent by God: "to teach humankind and to do justice and uprightness on the earth" (Jubilees 4:15). Only later do they sin with the daughters of men, and Enoch testifies against them (Jubilees 4:22). The change keeps the origin of evil in the angels' own choice. The story continues in Jubilees 5.

Jubilees 4:17-26 is the oldest summary of the Enoch traditions outside 1 Enoch. Enoch is the first human to learn writing (4:17); he records the signs of the sky and the calendar (4:17-18), sees the future in a dream (4:19), spends six jubilees with the angels (4:21), testifies against the Watchers (4:22), and is taken into Eden, where he writes down the judgment of the world (4:23). Charles (1902) matched these verses to 1 Enoch 6-16, 23-36 and 72-90.

Jubilees retells Genesis 1 by counting works: seven on the first day (including the angels), one on the second, four on the third (including Eden), three on the fourth, three on the fifth and four on the sixth, twenty-two in all (Jubilees 2:3-15). The number matches the twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob (Jubilees 2:23), and later Greek and Hebrew writers linked it to the twenty-two Hebrew letters.

Jubilees 2 retells Genesis 1:1-2:3 as dictated by an angel who saw it: "we saw his works, and we blessed him" (Jubilees 2:3). It adds the creation of the angels on the first day and the planting of Eden on the third, and makes the Sabbath the goal of creation.

Jubilees dates every step: the animals named in the second week, the woman made on the sixth day of that week, Adam brought into Eden after forty days and Eve after eighty (the reason for Leviticus 12), seven years in the garden, the Fall on the 17th of the second month, the expulsion on the first of the fourth, and Adam's death at 930, within the "day" of a thousand years (Jubilees 3:1-35; 4:29-30). Eve covers herself before she gives the fruit to Adam (Jubilees 3:21), and Adam burns incense as he leaves Eden (Jubilees 3:27).

sections.h: Eden as a sanctuary in Jubilees
sections.b: In Jubilees Eden is planted on the third day (2:7) and is "holier than all the earth" (3:12), so Adam and Eve may enter only after the days of purity a mother keeps before entering the sanctuary. It is one of the Lord's four holy places, with the Mountain of the East, Sinai and Zion (4:26). Enoch is taken there and writes the judgment of the world (4:23).

Jubilees names Cain's wife Awan, his sister, and dates the murder to the first year of the third jubilee. A law against secret murder is written on the heavenly tablets because of it (Jubilees 4:5). Cain dies in the same year as Adam, when his house falls on him: "with a stone he had killed Abel, and with a stone he was killed by a just judgment" (Jubilees 4:31).

sections.h: Jubilees 3: why forty and eighty days
sections.b: Leviticus 12 gives the days of purity after a birth without a reason. Jubilees 3:8-14 explains them from Eden: Adam was brought into the garden after forty days and Eve after eighty, so a mother of a boy waits forty days, and of a girl eighty, before touching holy things or entering the sanctuary.

Jubilees presents itself as revelation to Moses on Sinai, written beside the Torah (1:1-5, 26-27). It shows laws of the Torah already written on the heavenly tablets and given in Eden or to the first generations: the Sabbath (2:25-33), purity after childbirth (3:10-14), covering nakedness (3:31), the curse on secret murder (4:5) and punishment in kind (4:32).

sections.h: Jubilees: the book set on Sinai
sections.b: Jubilees opens in Exodus 24: Moses goes up the mountain on the sixteenth day of the third month, waits six days in the cloud, and stays forty days and nights (Jubilees 1:1-4). Everything that follows is what he heard there. Sinai is one of the Lord's four holy places (Jubilees 4:26).

sections.h: Jubilees 3: when the animals stopped talking
sections.b: Jubilees says all animals spoke one language until the day Adam left Eden, when their mouths were shut (Jubilees 3:28). Josephus (Antiquities 1.1.4) says the same. The snake of Genesis 3 is here just one of the speaking creatures.

sections.h: A day of a thousand years (Jubilees 4:30)
sections.b: Jubilees explains why Adam did not die the day he ate: "a thousand years are one day in the testimony of the heavens," and he died at 930, within that day (Jubilees 4:30). The same reckoning appears in Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8; Charles (1902) notes that Justin Martyr used the argument too.

Jubilees has Adam burn frankincense, galbanum, stacte and spices as he leaves Eden (Jubilees 3:27), and Enoch burn the evening incense of the sanctuary (Jubilees 4:25), long before the incense law of Exodus 30.
Jubilees 1:29 looks to the day when the heavens, the earth and all the lights are renewed, and the sanctuary of the Lord is built on Zion; through Zion the earth will be made holy (Jubilees 4:26).

sections.h: Jubilees 4: the wives of the first fathers
sections.b: Genesis names almost none of the first wives. Jubilees names them all: Cain, Seth and Enosh marry their sisters (Awan, Azura, Noam), Kenan his sister Mualeleth, and from Mahalalel on each patriarch marries a cousin (Jubilees 4:9-33). Jubilees 3:7 repeats Genesis 2:24.
